title: Canary in the Mine

post.author: u/lamproom_bersaba
post.title: I keep the lamp room at a coal mine. At 23:00 the board said 83 men were underground. Their lamps said 40.

blocks.text: I'm Bersaba. I keep the lamp room at Tolgarrick Colliery, the coal mine our town is named after. Going down, every miner takes his lamp off the charging rack and taps his tag on the tablet by my door, a small touch screen. That's a tag-in. Coming up, he hangs his lamp back and taps again: a tag-out. The board on my wall shows who is underground. If the mine ever has to be searched, that board is the list.

Shifts are ten hours, and each goes down two hours before the one it relieves comes up. The day shift comes up at 14:00. The back shift went down at 12:00 and comes up at 22:00. The night shift goes down at 20:00. So from 20:00 to 22:00, my door sees only tag-ins.

The board is kept by a program we call the tally. It runs on ten servers, computers whose job is to answer other machines. One would do; the safety rules want spares. Each tap goes to the next server in turn, so each one gets every tenth tap.

Eliakim, our developer, sends out every new version of the tally the same way. First one server, tally-10, gets it, like the canaries old miners carried down to warn them of gas. That first server is called the canary.
When a server can't save a tap, it writes an error in its log, its diary. If the canary's log shows no errors after an hour, the new version goes to the other nine. That step is called promoting it.
A program, the rollout tool, watches the canary's errors for that hour, then nothing.
The tablet shows a green tick the moment you tap, before the server answers. It assumes the tap was saved. Nobody at my door ever sees an error.

New starters begin with the day shift at 04:00 tomorrow, with new tags whose longer numbers the old tally can't read. So this release was urgent. Eliakim sent it out at 20:00, before he went home. Here is its rollout log. Each line shows the time, how many of the ten servers ran the new version, and the tag-ins, tag-outs and errors the new version had handled since 20:00:

20:00  new 1 of 10   in 0  out 0   errors 0   canary on tally-10
21:00  new 1 of 10   in 4  out 0   errors 0   promoted to all ten
22:02  new 10 of 10  in 4  out 11  errors 11
22:11  new 10 of 10  in 4  out 43  errors 43

At 23:00 Jabez, the night deputy, rang for the count, as he does every hour. The board said 83 underground: the night shift's 40 and the back shift's 43. I looked at the rack. The back shift's 43 lamps hung there, charging, their little lights on. The old brass tally board, where each man hangs a brass disc going down and takes it back coming up, agreed with the lamps: 40 below.
The board had 43 men in the dark. Their lamps were beside me.

Every release before tonight went out at 13:30, after Eliakim's morning checks. Its canary hour ran past 14:00, when the day shift comes up, so it always served tag-outs. Nobody planned that. What should Eliakim change before the next release?

blocks.label: tally_rollout_night.png

diagram.aria: 19:30 to 23:00. tally-10 runs the old version until 20:00, the new version as the canary from 20:00 to 21:00, and the new version after that. The other nine run the old version until 21:00 and the new version after. Tag-ins come from 20:01 to 20:11. There are no tag-outs until 22:02; they come from 22:02 to 22:12 and all fail. From 22:02 the board and the lamps disagree, and by 23:00 there are 43 ghosts.

blocks.caption: 19:30 to 23:00. The canary hour, 20:00 to 21:00, held the night shift's 40 tag-ins and not one tag-out; tally-10 served 4 of them and logged no error, so all ten got the new version at 21:00. The back shift's 43 tag-outs came from 22:02, all on the new version, and every one failed.

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Miners took canaries below because a bird stops singing before men feel the gas. A canary release works the same way: a small share first, judged on what it saw. Two words you'll hear. Blast radius: how much is hit if a change goes wrong. One server in ten is a blast radius of a tenth. And a feature flag: a switch inside the program that turns new code off without sending out a new version. So, questions. Tap by tap, what did tally-10 actually see in its hour? And on the day releases, what did the canary see that tonight's didn't?

replies.author: u/lamproom_bersaba
replies.text: Tally-10 served 4 tag-ins, 0 tag-outs, no errors. On a day release the canary was running at 14:00, when the day shift came up.

comments.author: u/bluegreen_ancrum
comments.text: Canaries are theatre. One server, one hour of watching, and look what it caught. Do it properly: blue-green. Keep two full sets of ten servers, blue on the old version and green on the new. Switch every tap to green at once, and if anything breaks, switch everything back to blue in one click. That one-click switch back is a rollback, and a fast rollback is all you need.

comments.author: u/test_first_blyth
comments.text: The failure is earlier than the canary. Automated tests are small programs that try a new version before it ships: they tap fake tags in and out and check every answer. One test that taps a tag out would have caught this on Eliakim's laptop. Write more of them and bugs like this never reach the lamp room.

reply.prompt: Eliakim can change how the tally's releases go out before the next one. What should he change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Use blue-green instead: switch all ten at once, and switch back fast if anything breaks.
options.verdict: A fast undo, and nothing looked broken
options.part2: Eliakim set up blue-green: a second set of ten servers and a switch, watched for an hour. We replayed tonight in the sim. At 20:00 all ten went to the new version at once, so all 40 night-shift tag-ins ran on it, not 4. Tag-ins worked, the hour was quiet, nothing switched back. From 22:02 all 43 tag-outs failed: board 83, lamps 40, 43 ghosts, the same record, with the whole mine on the new code from the start. Replayed at the usual 13:30, the switch back came at 14:03, after the first cage of 11 had already failed: 11 ghosts, where the canary left 1.
options.senior: Blue-green makes switching and switching back fast and clean, and it is a good way to make the final switch. But it decides on the same evidence as tonight's canary: if the watched time has no tag-outs, nothing looks broken and there is nothing to switch back from. And it sends every request to the new version at once, so its blast radius is everything. A canary limits how much is hit while you learn; blue-green limits how long an undo takes. Use a canary first, then switch.

options.text: Run every canary for two hours instead of one, so it has more time to show an error.
options.part2: Eliakim set every canary to two hours. In the sim's replay tally-10 ran from 20:00 to 22:00, served 4 tag-ins and 0 tag-outs, logged no error, and was promoted at 22:00. The back shift's cage reached the top at 22:02. All 43 tag-outs failed, and at 23:00 the board said 83 and the lamps 40: 43 ghosts again.
options.senior: A longer canary only helps if the extra time brings the traffic the change touches. Time stands in for traffic, and at night it stands in badly: the hour after 20:00 has no tag-outs, and neither does the next. Judge a canary by what it has served on each path the change touches, not by the clock.

options.text: Promote the canary only once it has served enough tag-outs and tag-ins, not on time.
options.part2: Eliakim changed the rule: tally-10 is promoted only after it has served at least 3 tag-ins and 3 tag-outs with no error, however long that takes. In the sim's replay it was still the canary at 21:00, with 4 tag-ins and 0 tag-outs, waiting. At 22:02 the back shift's first cage came up, and the tenth man's tag-out went to tally-10 and failed. The rule rolled tally-10 back to the old version at 22:03, and the other 42 tagged out on the old version. At 23:00 the board said 41 and the lamps 40; the one extra name was in tally-10's log, and I marked him out by hand against his lamp. At 04:00 I wrote the new starters onto the brass board and the tally by hand. Eliakim fixed tag-out and sent the release out again at 13:30, with the new tag-out code behind a feature flag. One ghost instead of 43.
options.senior: Promote on evidence, not on time. Before a canary is widened, it should have served enough real traffic on every path the change touches, here tag-ins and tag-outs, with an error rate no worse than the old servers. The cost: a quiet path can make a release wait for hours, and the canary's own share is still hit, 1 tag-out in 43 tonight. That is what a canary is for: a small blast radius while you learn.

options.text: Add more automated tests before each release, so a tag-out bug can never ship again.
options.verdict: Earlier checks, the same blind rule
options.part2: Eliakim added tests that tap tags in and out before every release, and tonight's bug fails them, so this one would have stayed on his laptop. But the rollout rule did not change, so the sim's replay runs exactly as built: the canary saw 4 tag-ins and 0 tag-outs, was promoted at 21:00, and any tag-out bug the tests miss still makes 43 ghosts by 23:00. Better tests, the same blind canary.
options.senior: Tests catch the bugs you thought to test for, on test data. They are cheap and early, so keep adding them. But they don't replace watching the real thing, with real tags, real records and real timing. The canary is the last check on real traffic, and it should be judged on whether it has seen each path, not on silence.

sim.title: Run the Tolgarrick lamp room through a release
sim.lede: You're Eliakim, replaying the release from 19:00 to 23:00, one minute per tick. Ten tally servers take taps in turn, so tally-10 gets every tenth. Shifts are ten hours: day 04:00 to 14:00 (44 miners), back 12:00 to 22:00 (43), night 20:00 to 06:00 (40), and the cage brings 11 at a time. The new version saves tag-ins and fails every tag-out; the tablet shows a green tick either way. Pick the release time (20:00 tonight, or the usual 13:30), a canary or blue-green, the length, the promotion rule and the feature flag for the new tag-out code, and roll back all ten whenever you like. A ghost is a name on the board whose lamp is on the rack.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to 23:00 as built. Tally-10 serves 4 tag-ins and 0 tag-outs, is promoted at 21:00, and from 22:02 all 43 tag-outs fail: board 83, lamps 40, 43 ghosts. Roll back all ten: still 43 ghosts. Now each reply. Two hours: promoted at 22:00, 43 ghosts. Blue-green: all 40 tag-ins on the new version, no switch back, 43 ghosts. By traffic: still the canary at 21:00, rolled back at 22:03, 1 ghost. More tests leave the rollout as built. Then the usual 13:30: the canary catches it at 14:02 by luck, 1 ghost; blue-green there leaves 11. Last, switch the flag off: 0 ghosts.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke the rule; the rule was blind. The canary was judged by an hour of time, and the hour it got, 20:00 to 21:00, held tag-ins and no tag-outs at all. It saw 4 taps on the one path that worked, logged no error and was promoted to all ten, so the back shift's 43 tag-outs at 22:02 fell on broken code while every tablet showed a green tick.

steps.title: How a canary release works.
steps.text: First the new version goes to one server of ten, tally-10. Taps are dealt to the servers in turn, which engineers call round robin, so it gets every tenth tap. Then the rollout tool watches tally-10's errors. If it logs an error, the tool rolls it back: tally-10 gets the old version again, and only its tenth was hit. If the hour passes with none, the tool promotes the version to all ten. What can go wrong: every step judges only the taps the canary actually got. An hour with no errors on a path nobody used says nothing about that path.

steps.title: What tally-10 saw.
steps.text: From 20:00 to 21:00 the night shift went down in four cages: 40 tag-ins, of which tally-10 served 4, and not one tag-out, because the back shift was still below. The bug was in tag-out only, so the canary had nothing to fail on. At 21:00 it was promoted. The back shift's cage came up from 22:02 to 22:11, and all 43 tag-outs reached the new version. Each one wrote an error in a log nobody was watching, and each tablet showed its green tick before the server answered. At 23:00 the board said 83 and the lamps 40.

steps.title: Why it worked before.
steps.text: Every earlier release went out at 13:30, so its canary hour ran across the 14:00 shift change and served the day shift's tag-outs. Nobody chose that; it was luck. In the sim, tonight's release sent at 13:30 is caught at 14:02, when tally-10's first tag-out fails, and rolled back at 14:03, with 1 ghost. Moving the release to 20:00 didn't change the rule. It removed the luck. And the day slot was blind the other way: its hour had no tag-ins at all, so a tag-in bug would have been promoted just as quietly.

steps.title: Blue-green, feature flags and rollbacks.
steps.text: Blue-green keeps two full sets of servers, switches all traffic from old to new at once, and switches back if needed (Spinnaker calls it red/black). The undo is fast, but everything is on the new code at once. A feature flag is a switch inside the program: with the new tag-out code switched off, the release goes out and tag-outs use the old code, with no new deploy, and in the sim there are 0 ghosts. A rollback puts the old version back. It does not mend what the new one did: rolled back at 23:00, the board still has 43 ghosts.

steps.title: Blast radius, and what should promote a canary.
steps.text: Blast radius is how much is hit if a change goes wrong: one server in ten for a canary, all ten for blue-green. A canary keeps it small while it gathers evidence, so promote on evidence: enough real taps on every path the change touches, here at least 3 tag-ins and 3 tag-outs with no error (on a busy service, an error rate no worse than the old servers). The cost is waiting. Tonight the canary would have waited until 22:02, failed on the tenth man's tag-out and rolled back, with 1 ghost.

diagram.aria: The fix. Taps go from the lamp-room tablet to the load balancer, which sends 1 in 10 to tally-10, the canary on the new version, and 9 in 10 to tally-01 to 09 on the old version. The canary's counts go to the promotion rule: 3 tag-ins and 3 tag-outs, and no errors. An error rolls tally-10 back, at 22:03 tonight, with 1 ghost. A feature flag can switch the new tag-out code off on every server without a deploy.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for the next release. Tally-10 gets the new version and every tenth tap. It is promoted only after it has served 3 tag-ins and 3 tag-outs with no error; an error rolls it back. In the sim's replay of tonight: still the canary at 21:00, rolled back at 22:03 after the tenth man's tag-out failed, 1 ghost instead of 43. The feature flag can switch the new tag-out code off without a deploy.

fix.title: The fix: promote on traffic on every path, not on time
fix.text: List the paths the change touches: here, tag-in and tag-out. Give the new version to one server, and promote it only after it has served enough real traffic on each of those paths with no errors: at least 3 tag-ins and 3 tag-outs tonight, and on a busy service an error rate no worse than the old servers. Any error rolls the canary back at once. If a path is quiet, the release waits; that is the price. Put risky new code behind a feature flag, so it can be switched off without a deploy, and keep blue-green for the final switch if you like it. In the sim's replay of tonight: still the canary at 21:00, rolled back at 22:03, 1 ghost instead of 43.

limits: A traffic rule needs someone to list the paths a change touches. Miss one, such as a lamp reported lost, which might happen a few times a year, and the canary is promoted without ever trying it. For rare paths, use a test run against the real system or keep the code behind a flag.

A rollback changes code, not records. Every tag-out the new version failed stays wrong on the board until someone mends it, and a version that changes how records are stored can leave records the old version cannot read.
The canary's own share is still hit: 1 tag-out in 43 tonight. A smaller share means less harm and slower evidence.

head: Rollout
Good
Bad
rows: Simple; a tenth of taps at risk for the hour.
More time to see errors on busy paths.
Promoted at 22:00, still before the first tag-out: 43 ghosts.
Fast, clean switch and switch back.
Every tap on the new code at once; nothing looked broken: 43 ghosts. At 13:30, 11.
Canary by traffic on every path
Waits for tag-outs: rolled back at 22:03, 1 ghost.
A quiet path makes the release wait; someone must list the paths.
Catches known bugs before any miner taps.
The rollout is unchanged; a bug the tests miss still makes 43 ghosts.
Feature flag on new tag-out code
Switch it off without a deploy: 0 ghosts.
Flags pile up and must be cleaned out; an old flag reused can wake old code.

explain.seniorTake: A deployment strategy is a way of spending risk. A canary spends a small blast radius to buy evidence, blue-green buys a fast undo, a feature flag buys a switch you can flip without a deploy, and a rollback buys back the old code but not the damage done. None of them works if you judge it on silence. Decide what evidence a change must earn before it spreads: real traffic on every path it touches, with errors no worse than the old version, and treat time only as a ceiling, never as proof. Then remember what each tool cannot undo: records the new version wrote, and the people who were told yes by a screen that never checked.

realWorld.title: CrowdStrike, July 2024: one update, every machine online
realWorld.text: CrowdStrike, a security company whose program runs on customers' computers, says in its Preliminary Post Incident Review that "On Friday, July 19, 2024 at 04:09 UTC" (UTC is the world's reference clock) a content update went out, that Windows hosts running sensor version 7.11 and above which were online between 04:09 UTC and 05:27 UTC and received the update were affected, and that "The defect in the content update was reverted on Friday, July 19, 2024 at 05:27 UTC." Among its changes: "Implement a staggered deployment strategy for Rapid Response Content in which updates are gradually deployed to larger portions of the sensor base, starting with a canary deployment."

realWorld.title: CrowdStrike root cause analysis: promoted ring by ring
realWorld.text: The External Technical Root Cause Analysis lists as a finding: "Each Template Instance should be deployed in a staged rollout." It goes on: "New Template Instances that have passed canary testing are to be successively promoted to wider deployment rings or rolled back if problems are detected." Each promotion "is followed by additional bake-in time, where telemetry is gathered". It also gives customers control: "Customers can choose where and when Rapid Response Content updates are deployed."

realWorld.title: Knight Capital, August 2012: seven of eight servers, and an old flag
realWorld.text: The order of the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) says Knight Capital's new code for the Retail Liquidity Program (RLP), sent to SMARS, its automated order router, "repurposed a flag that was formerly used to activate the Power Peg code", functionality it had stopped using years earlier. During the deployment "one of Knight's technicians did not copy the new code to one of the eight SMARS computer servers", and "Knight did not have a second technician review this deployment". On August 1 the eighth server ran the old code for orders carrying the flag: "4 million executions in 154 stocks for more than 397 million shares in approximately 45 minutes", and "Ultimately, Knight realized a $460 million loss on these positions."

realWorld.title: Knight Capital: the rollback that made it worse
realWorld.text: The same order says that while staff hunted for the cause, "Knight uninstalled the new RLP code from the seven servers where it had been deployed correctly. This action worsened the problem, causing additional incoming parent orders to activate the Power Peg code that was present on those servers". A rollback puts old code back; if the old code is the danger, it spreads it.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.8.32
realWorld.text: Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022 has a control titled Change management (A.8.32). The control wording is in the standard itself; the linked page is a secondary guide that names and explains it.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022, A.8.9
realWorld.text: The same Annex A has a control titled Configuration management (A.8.9), covering how a system's settings are recorded and controlled. The control wording is in the standard itself; the linked page is a secondary guide.

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC8.1: controlled changes
realWorld.text: SOC 2's criterion CC8.1 begins: "The entity authorizes, designs, develops or acquires, configures, documents, tests, approves, and implements changes", and goes on to cover changes to infrastructure, data, software and procedures. A release promoted on an hour that never tried the changed path is a change that was not really tested.

asked: Canary or blue-green: when would you use each?
interview.answer: Blast radius is how much is affected if a change goes wrong: which users, which share of traffic, which systems. Deployment strategies are ways of controlling it. A canary sends a new version to a small share first, often one server or a few percent of traffic, and widens it only on evidence; it keeps the blast radius small while you learn. Blue-green runs two full environments and moves all traffic from old to new at once, with a fast switch back; it makes the cutover and the undo clean, but everything is on the new code at the same moment, so its blast radius is everything. In practice you combine them: canary first, then blue-green or a rolling switch for the rest. A canary should be promoted on evidence, not on time: enough real traffic on each path the change touches, with error rate and latency no worse than the old version, compared side by side, and time only as a ceiling. A canary judged by time can be promoted on a quiet hour that never used the changed path. A story I'd tell: a mine's tally service released at 20:00, when miners were only going down; the canary saw tag-ins and no tag-outs, was promoted after an hour with no errors, and the back shift's 43 tag-outs all failed. Promoting only after the canary had served tag-outs would have rolled it back on the first failure, with one person affected. I'd add feature flags, so new code can be switched off without a deploy, and remember that a rollback restores code, not data, which is why Knight Capital's 2012 rollback made things worse.

atWork: Look at your last few releases and ask what the canary actually saw before it was promoted. It is a common pattern: a canary promoted on a quiet hour that never used the changed path, such as a nightly release whose canary saw no logins, no refunds or no batch jobs. Check three things. Does your promotion rule count requests on each path the change touches, or only minutes? Does it compare the canary's error rate with the old servers', side by side? And is risky new code behind a feature flag, so it can be switched off without a deploy? Then check your rollback: when did you last roll back on purpose, and what did it leave behind in your data? Build Night G7 (TLS, HTTP/2, hot reload) uses this case's rollback habit: keep the previous version ready, and know what a rollback does not undo. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.8.32 (Change management) and A.8.9 (Configuration management) apply, and if it is pursuing SOC 2, CC8.1 expects changes to be authorized, tested and approved in a controlled way. Writing down what evidence promotes a release, and keeping the rollout's record, builds that in now instead of at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team changes how the shop's checkout handles refunds. The release goes out at 09:00 as a canary on 1 of 20 servers, is watched for 30 minutes with zero errors, and is promoted to all 20. By 15:00, every refund is failing. Refund requests almost all arrive in the afternoon. What went wrong with the rollout, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The canary saw no refund requests in its 30 minutes, so its zero errors proved nothing about the changed path
Promote on traffic on every changed path, such as a minimum number of refunds with no errors, not on time
Put the new refund code behind a feature flag so it can be switched off without a deploy, and keep the blast radius small

recall.model: The canary never saw a refund. It ran from 09:00 to 09:30, and refunds arrive in the afternoon, so its zero errors said nothing about the path the change touched; it was promoted on silence, and by afternoon all 20 servers had the broken code. I'd promote by traffic, not by time: list the paths the change touches, and require a minimum number of refunds served by the canary, with an error rate no worse than the old servers, before it widens, with time only as a ceiling. A canary that waits until the first afternoon refunds would have failed on one server in twenty and rolled back. I'd also put the new refund code behind a feature flag, so it can be switched off without a deploy, which keeps the blast radius small even if something slips through.

recall.prompt: What does blast radius mean in deployments?
options: How much is affected if a change goes wrong
How many servers a load balancer can reach
recall.why: Blast radius is how much is hit when a change is bad: users, traffic or systems. A canary on one server of ten keeps it to a tenth while you learn; blue-green switches everything at once, so its blast radius is all of it.

recall.prompt: Which statement about blue-green and canary releases is true?
options: Blue-green limits how much is hit; a canary limits how long the undo takes
Blue-green gives a fast switch back but moves everything at once; a canary limits how much is hit while evidence comes in
Both send the new version to a small share first
A canary needs two full sets of servers
recall.why: Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches all traffic at once, with a fast switch back. A canary sends a small share first and widens it on evidence. Many teams use a canary first and a blue-green switch for the rest.

recall.prompt: A canary ran for an hour with no errors and is about to be promoted. Which question matters most first?
options: Did it run for at least an hour?
Did it serve real traffic on every path the change touches?
Is the release tagged with a version number?
Is the old version still installed somewhere?
recall.why: No errors only means something if the canary used the changed code. Tolgarrick's canary had an error-free hour of tag-ins and not one tag-out, and the bug was in tag-out.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Promotion by traffic has worked all spring. In March Eliakim released a version that also changed how tag-ins are stored. It went out at 20:00 as a canary on tally-10, which served 4 of the night shift's tag-ins, stored the new way, and waited. At 22:02 a back-shift man's tag-out failed on tally-10, because the new version couldn't find his tag-in, stored the old way at 12:00; tally-10 was rolled back at 22:03, as designed, and I marked him out by hand. Then at 06:00 the night shift came up. Four men tapped out, got their green ticks and stayed on the board. Their lamps were on the rack. The other 36 were fine.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why are four men still on the board after a rollback that worked, and what should Eliakim change?

keyIdeas.idea: The rollback put the old code back but not the four records the canary wrote in the new form, which the old version cannot read
Make storage changes backward compatible in steps: first every version reads both forms, and only then does the new one write the new form
Rehearse the rollback on the canary and keep the new storage behind a feature flag, or mend the records a rollback strands

coldCase.model: The rollback worked on the code and did nothing to the data. Tally-10 wrote the four night-shift tag-ins in the new form, and when it went back to the old version, those records stayed; at 06:00 the old version cannot read them, so their tag-outs failed and the green ticks lied again. The same mismatch, the other way round, failed the back-shift man at 22:02. A rollback doesn't undo what the new version wrote. The fix is to make storage changes backward compatible in steps: first release a version that reads both forms and still writes the old one, let it spread everywhere, and only then release the one that writes the new form, so any version can read any record and a rollback is safe. Keep the new storage behind a feature flag, rehearse the rollback on the canary before trusting it, and when a rollback does strand records, mend the records the same night rather than at 06:00.
